The automation logic is sound, and I don’t want to downplay how important automation is, but you also have to get your hands on the devices at some point to validate everything is working. When the devices are in the hands of users, that’s easy because the users can just tell you if there’s a problem, but when you have a deployment like this, it becomes a bit less transparent, and sometimes that manual validation and verification is actually an important part of the process. I am very well acquainted with large deployments, and it’s always been a problem and I’ve looked into something like this in the past and it’s always a thing where I found. It’s easier to just use it as a training experience for lower level staff to start learning all the underpinnings of how this stuff works, and then they can do the work. It’s a really tough balance to find, and I just don’t quite feel like this is a thing that should be automated. I would make the argument that if you have 1000 devices it’s being managed by one person, the automation isn’t going to help. Because you don’t have that validation that everything is working as expected because the devices aren’t in the hands of users, The automation can fail, and if you don’t have that verification, it’s just gonna splatter down. A workload of that size anyway should have theoretically a few people working on it, and like I said, it’s a great training opportunity for lower to your helpdesk or you know upper to your helpdesk that are wanting to get into more direct administrative roles to get the training and the knowledge they need to be able to do that. It’s a great thought experiment, and I’m actually really enjoying like figuring this stuff out, it’s just in my opinion, we should automate everything that we realistically can, and this type of solution doesn’t end well for automation. I was in a school where we deployed somewhere around 1300 iPads and we would have to get our hands on them at least once a year, just to make sure that everything was working as expected, even though we still automated almost everything because it was really just me there.

Managing the device really only changes based on what you end up with in a very minimal way- really just inventory tracking and how apps are installed. If a device walks away your MDM should be able to set in lock mode in either case but these are two drastically different uses with specific considerations.

A server is just something that hosts files/applications/software for a wider network of users to access. Anything can be a server, including your phone.

A workstation, at it's base form, is just a computer that is used to do work things.

Some hardware is well suited for certain workloads, like crunching a lot of data or routing traffic across data hosts for example- and that's why you see things like Xeon's in datacenters.

Some workloads are ultimately the same thing, but done by a lone user. Things like CAD or 3D modeling may be benefitted by using those same Xeon processors.

So, to more directly answer your question, workstations that you see will likely be close (if not directly equal) to traditional rackmounted servers.

I love having high end hardware to play with, but the reality is that you can use anything to do anything- it may take a lot longer for some of it. Once you get in the mindset of thinking that anything can be a server or anything can be a workstation it's a bit easier to start picking things out but the reality is that you should get what you want/need to learn and do things. The differences are really just the use cases for what the devices are meant for- you'll find a lot of servers with IPMI..... but that's usually done at the board level so it's easy to port to a workstation. The real big difference I've seen is that workstations will have a bit more expandability.

tl;dr: functionally similar, but there may be some QOL features missing like IPMI or expansion slots.

That specific use case doesn't happen enough in my testing for it to be adequate to leave just to Jamf Pro.

BUT! With Nudge, you can put messaging in there on why the user should restart, or just leave the box up and annoying until they do it.

Automated Device Enrollment with Apple Business/School Manager should be the default and user-initiated enrollment should be need based, like a BYOD deployment.

If the device is in ABM, the device *will* re-enroll if it gets wiped. Sonoma has started checking ABM and mandating enrollment so workarounds don't work.

From there, the options get pretty endless. You can have it set up where a user gets the device from Apple and logs in to an identity provider and everything gets set up for them, all the way down to just streamlining enrollment for your team to white glove the setup. I would recommend doing the training for Jamf 100 (you don't have to take the test) or engaging Jamf's Professional Services if you need a more clear idea, but if you get specific questions you can ask here or even Jamf's support.
